The G-body: the shape that learned to travel

Everyone else builds on the 964. We build on the car before it, for three reasons: the shell is galvanised, the supply is honest, and every weakness it has is already known and already solved.

The fashionable donor for a reimagined 911 is the 964. It is the car the best-known houses use, and there are good reasons for that: later engineering, a stiffer shell, more modern brakes.

We build on the car before it. Not because it is cheaper, though it is, but because for a car that is meant to be driven a long way in a hard climate it is the better foundation. Three reasons, in order of importance.

One: the shell is galvanised

From the mid-1970s the 911 body shell was hot-dip galvanised. For a car that will live in salt air, be driven on unsealed roads and spend forty more years outdoors, that is the single most consequential fact about it.

A restoration is only as durable as what it is built on. Paint, trim and mechanicals can all be renewed. A shell that has begun to go cannot be, not honestly, and not at a price anyone should pay. Starting with galvanised steel means the work we do has somewhere permanent to sit.

Two: the supply is honest

Roughly 74,000 3.2 Carreras and 60,000 SCs were built. That depth matters in a way that is easy to underrate: it means we can reject cars.

A thin donor market forces compromise. When there are only a handful of candidates, a car with marginal rust becomes tempting, and rectification beyond a certain threshold destroys the economics of the whole build. With a deep market we hold a quality floor instead, and walk away.

The price difference is real but it is not the argument. It matters because every dollar not spent on the donor is available for engineering and craftsmanship, which is what a client is actually paying for.

Three: the weaknesses are known

This is the part that reassures engineers and unsettles everyone else, so it is worth saying plainly. The G-body has a specific, finite, well-documented list of weak points. All of them have known fixes, most of them from the factory itself.

A known problem with a known solution is not a risk. It is a line item.

What we change, and why

  • Timing-chain tensioners. Pre-1984 cars use a non-pressure-fed design that is the engine's best-known failure point. Replaced with the factory's own pressure-fed Carrera-style tensioner and oil feed.
  • The CIS airbox. A backfire can split it. A pop-off valve resolves it permanently.
  • The clutch centre. The original rubber-centred design perishes. Replaced with a sprung centre.
  • Dilavar head studs. They fatigue on high-mileage engines. Replaced during the rebuild, not inspected and hoped over.
  • The 915 gearbox. Notchy synchros are characteristic rather than faulty, and a full rebuild transforms the shift without changing the character.
  • Oil lines. Forty-year-old lines are replaced entirely. All of them.

Our donor window is 1979 to 1985, and the gearbox is part of the reason. It keeps the car in the classic silhouette, before the later transmission, in the period with the widest supply.

What we do not do

We do not chase peak power. Output lands between 210 and 260 kW, specified for mid-range torque rather than a headline figure, because mid-range is what a long drive on an open road actually uses.

There is a capacity arms race in this segment. We are not in it. Taste, provenance, drivability and story are the axes worth competing on.

The bodywork follows the same logic. Arches are flared 25 to 40 millimetres, which is enough for the wheel and tyre the car needs and not a millimetre more. Panel gaps are held to 3.5 millimetres plus or minus 0.5, measured and recorded rather than eyeballed.

The result

A car that looks like the one you remember, because it is. It simply stops doing the specific things that made the original frustrating, and it does so in a way that a future owner can verify, line by line, from the record.
